47-009.r: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay → among the first graduates of Calcutta University (with Joddu Nath Bose); 'Sitaram' was his last novel. Both correct.

47-010.r: 'Vande Mataram' → Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, from his novel 'Anand Math' (on the Sanyasi Revolt); first sung by Tagore at the Calcutta Congress session, 1896.

47-012.r: Theme of 'Anandmath' → Sanyasi Revolt; sanyasis rose after British rule, the 1770 famine and a ban on pilgrimage. Bankim made the revolt famous.

47-016.r: Correct years: Pabna revolt 1873-76; Deccan Kisan revolt 1875; Sanyasi revolt 1763-1800 (not 1894); Kol uprising 1831-32 (not 1870).
47-016.c: Answer not printed; by the explanation both (c) Sanyasi 1894 and (d) Kol 1870 are wrong pairs.

47-017.r: Barhiya Tal resistance (Munger) → demand to restore Bakasht land.

47-018.r: Chief centre of the Wahabi Movement → Patna; led by Syed Ahmad Barelvi, inspired by Abdul Wahab of Arabia and Shah Waliullah of Delhi; Islamic revivalist.

47-019.r: Kuka Movement (Punjab) → led by Guru Ram Singh; begun in the 1840s by Bhagat Jawahar Mal (Sian Sahib) to purify Sikhism; turned anti-British.

47-021.r: Pagalpanthi rebellion → Garo tribe; sect founded by Karam (Karim) Shah of North Bengal; his son Tipu Shah captured Sherpur in 1825.

47-023.r: Farazi rebellion → led by Dadu (Dudu) Miyan, son of founder Haji Shariatullah (Faridpur, Bengal); later merged with the Wahabis.
47-023.t: Faraizis = followers of Haji Shariatullah; Pagalpanthis = Karam Shah.

47-025.r: Velu Thampi → revolt in Travancore (Kerala) after Wellesley forced Subsidiary Alliance (1805) and the British Resident behaved rudely; backed by the Nair battalion.

47-026.r: Ganjam revolt (1800-1805) led by Dhananjay; Gumsur revolt (1808-1837) first under Shrikar Bhanja, then son Dhananjay Bhanja II → (i), (ii), (iii) true; Dhananjay was son, not father.

47-027.r: Ramosi Krishak Jatha → Vasudeo Balwant Phadke (1845-83); turned Ramoshi tribals into a fighting force; died 1883 on hunger strike in Kala Pani.

47-028.r: Ramosi uprising → Western Ghats; Ramoshi hill tribes rose in 1822 under Chittur Singh around Satara, again 1825-1826; unrest till 1831-32.

47-029.r: Gadkari rebellion → Kolhapur, 1844; Gadkaris were hereditary fort servants of the Marathas, angered by land revenue policies.

47-030.r: Khonds revolted (1846-1855) when the British banned the Meriah (human sacrifice) and imposed new taxes; leader Chakra Bisoi.

47-031.r: Kol Revolt → led by Budhu (Buddho) Bhagat in Chhota Nagpur, 1831-32.

47-032.r: Kol Mutiny 1831 (Buddho Bhagat) → Singhbhum, Chhotanagpur (also Ranchi, Hazaribagh, Palamu, Manbhum); against outsider moneylenders and farmers after new land laws.

47-033.r: Waghera uprising → Okhamandal region, against the Gaekwad of Baroda backed by the British; raids 1818-1819, peace 1820; rose again 1858-59.
47-033.c: Answer not printed; explanation links it to Baroda's Gaekwad (Okhamandal), i.e. option (d).

47-034.r: Order: Sepoy mutiny in Bengal (1764, a battalion at Buxar joined Mir Qasim) → Vellore (1806) → Kutch (1816-32) → Kol (1831-1832) → Santhal (1855-56).

47-035.r: Vellore Mutiny (1806) → during Governor-General Sir George Barlow (1805-1807); sepoys resented interference in social and religious customs.

47-036.r: No revolt is named 'Chhotanagpur Tribal Revolt'; region's revolts: Cheron 1800, Ho 1820-21, Kol 1831-32, Santhal 1855-56, Munda 1899-1900.
47-036.c: Answer not printed; book says if the Ho revolt (1820-21) is meant, option (b) 1820.

47-037.r: Tribal rebellion against the British → Bihar: Munda and Ho tribes of Chhotanagpur (Ho 1820-21) fought the British army in 1831; unrest till 1837.

47-038.r: Santhal rebellion (1855-56) → four brothers Sidhu, Kanhu, Chand and Bhairav, against the British revenue system.

47-045.r: Wrong pair: Ahom - 1815 → Ahom revolt 1828 (Gomdhar Kunwar). Correct: Khasi 1829-33 (Tirot Singh); Kol 1831-1832 (Buddho Bhagat); Santhal 1855-56.

47-046.r: Santhals defeated Major Burrough in 1855; their real enemy was the 'Dikus' (outsider officials); ten thousand met at Bhognadih on 30 June 1855.

47-047.r: Santhal Hool (from 30 June 1855): Major Burrough (Baroz) lost near Bhagalpur; Gokko led in Godda; Mahajan Deen Dayal Rai figures in it → 1, 2, 3 correct.

47-048.r: After the Santhal uprising → separate Santhal Pargana district created; Santhal Pargana Tenancy Act made land transfer to non-Santhals illegal. Both correct.

47-049.r: Santhal Pargana in ancient times → 'Narikhand'; Buddhist texts call it 'Kajangala'; in the Mahabharata period part of Anga Mahajanapada.

47-050.r: Uprising in Maharashtra → Bhil uprising (1818-31) in the Khandesh hills, after British occupation of Khandesh (1818); Trimbakji, Baji Rao II's minister, allegedly instigated it.

47-051.r: Lasodia Movement for social reform among Bhils (Mewar, Vagad) → Govind Giri, founder of 'Samp Sabha' (1883); Surji Bhagat also involved.

47-052.r: Ulgulan revolt → Birsa Munda (1899-1900); 'Great Tumult' aiming at an independent Munda Raj as Khuntkatti land rights were eroded.

47-053.r: 'Ulgulan' (Great Tumult) → Birsa Munda's revolt, 1899-1900, for Munda Raj and tribal rights over land taken by landlords, moneylenders and British.

47-054.r: 'Dharti Aaba' (Father of the Earth) → Birsa Munda, born 1875; claimed to be a prophet in 1895; led the revivalist Munda rebellion.

47-057.r: Munda rebellion under Birsa Munda → 1899; Mundas' Khuntkatti system was being eroded by jagirdars, thikedars and moneylenders.
47-057.c: The book dates the rebellion to 1899, not an option; but its explanation says Birsa declared himself a prophet in 1895, when his movement began, which is option (d).

47-058.r: Birsa Munda captured asleep → 3 February 1900, Jamkopai forest, Chakradharpur (West Singhbhum); died in prison on 9 June 1900.

47-059.r: Birsa Munda wanted an independent Munda Raj, not a separate state like Jharkhand → 'None of these'; revolt at Ranchi, 1899-1900.

47-060.r: Birsa Munda's working area → Ranchi (extending to Bhagalpur); urged Mundas to drop superstitions, animal sacrifice and intoxicants.

47-062.r: Word 'Adivasi' first used for tribal people → Thakkar Bappa (Amritlal Vithaldas Thakkar), member of the Servants of India Society.

47-063.r: Common factor behind 19th-century tribal revolts → complete disruption of the tribes' old agrarian order; new revenue, missionaries and moneylenders were contributory causes.

47-064.r: Ho (Hoz) revolt → 1820-21, in then Bihar (now Jharkhand).

47-065.r: Khairwar tribal movement → 1874, led by Bhagirath Manjhi.

47-066.r: Anti-British revolts in Sambalpur → Surendra Sai, claimant to the Sambalpur throne; surrendered in 1862.

47-067.r: Order: Santhal Rebellion (1855-56) → Sepoy Mutiny (1857) → Indigo Revolt (1859-60) → Deccan Riot (1875).

47-068.r: Immediate cause of the Deccan Riots (1875) → shadow of famine and high interest charged by Mahajans; more than one option correct.

47-069.r: After 1857 → Indigo Revolt (1859-60), Deccan Agriculturists Riots (1875), Birsa Munda Uprising (1899-1900); Santhal Rebellion (1855-56) came before.

47-070.r: Moplah revolt → Kerala (Malabar, 1921); Pabna revolt → Bengal (1873-76); Eka Movement → Oudh (1921-22); Birsa Munda revolt → Bihar (now Jharkhand).

47-072.r: Bengal Indigo Revolt → 1859-60; Pabna Peasant Revolt → 1873-76; Mopla Rebellion → 1921; Tebhaga Movement → 1946-47.
47-072.c: Answer not printed; book dates Pabna 1873-76, not the listed 1879-80; otherwise option (d) fits.
